title: No need to hide
hook: if you've judged it right, don't hide doing it (Enchiridion 35)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was two pictures: the enjoying, and the regret after. Your line was wait.

A teenager in a school cafeteria sees the new kid eating alone. She'd like to go sit with him. She'd also like nobody to see her do it. A man leaves the office at five sharp to coach his daughter's soccer team, and slips out the side door so the others won't notice. People do the right thing, and then do it a little in hiding, as if they've been caught. Section thirty-five of the Enchiridion is only a few lines long, and it's aimed at exactly that side door.
screen: `THE NEW KID EATING ALONE.` → `OUT THE SIDE DOOR AT FIVE.` → `NO NEED TO HIDE.`

segments.voice: When you've judged that something ought to be done, and you're doing it, Epictetus says, never avoid being seen doing it, even if the many are going to think badly of it. The logic is tidy. Either the thing is wrong, or it's right. If it's wrong, don't do it at all. If it's right, the people who'll find fault with it are mistaken, so why be afraid of them? Hiding a right action quietly hands a vote to people whose opinion, by your own judgment, is wrong. It echoes earlier sections. Section thirteen asked you to be content to seem foolish about outside things, and section twenty-two warned that anyone who takes up this way of life will be laughed at. Today is the practical follow-through. You've already accepted that people may think you odd. So stop ducking. There's a test hidden in the sentence, too. If you notice the urge to hide something you're doing, ask why. Sometimes it's only fear of what people will say, and his answer is: then do it in the open. But sometimes the wish to hide is the first quiet sign that the thing isn't right, and his answer to that is just as plain: then don't do it. This isn't about showing off; the handbook gets to that soon. It's about not shrinking. A right thing done openly also gives the next person permission to do it too.
screen: `JUDGED RIGHT? DON'T AVOID BEING SEEN.` · `WRONG: DON'T. RIGHT: WHY FEAR CRITICS?` · `YOU'VE ALREADY ACCEPTED SEEMING ODD.` · `THE URGE TO HIDE IS A TEST.` · then, large: `NO NEED TO HIDE.`

segments.voice: Think of one right thing you do a little sheepishly: leaving on time for your family, saying no to a drink, bowing your head before a meal, asking a question in a meeting, sitting with someone others avoid. Picture yourself doing it in plain view, at an ordinary pace, with no apology and no announcement. Notice whether the urge to hide shows up, and what it's made of.
The many. Epictetus' name for the people whose disapproval needn't be feared; if you've judged it right, don't avoid being seen doing it. Today's word.
Your line: without the side door. If it's right, the front door works fine. Day three hundred seventy.

howItsDone: People practicing Stoicism sometimes check whether they are hiding a right action out of fear of disapproval, and if so, do it openly; if the wish to hide signals that the act is wrong, they don't do it.

chat.says: I want to sit with the new kid at lunch, but people might think I'm weird.
options: If it's right, Epictetus says don't hide it; the ones who'd mock it are mistaken.
Epictetus would say wait until nobody's watching, so no one thinks less of you.
He'd say do it only if your friends agree, since the crowd decides what's right.
chat.meaning: If a thing is wrong, don't do it; if it's right, why fear those who wrongly find fault? Don't avoid being seen doing it.

the many.meaning: Epictetus' term for the crowd and its opinions

Epictetus.meaning: the Stoic teacher whose sayings make up the handbook

Enchiridion.meaning: the handbook: a short collection of Epictetus' teachings

notes: Enchiridion 35 paraphrased: when you do a thing judged right, never avoid being seen doing it, even if the many form an unfavorable opinion; if not right, avoid doing it; if right, why fear those who wrongly censure you. Confirm.
The 'urge to hide is a test' is a reading drawn from the 'if it is not right, avoid doing it' clause; confirm it is fair.
Greek οἱ πολλοί: confirm it appears in Ench. 35 and the 'hoi polloi' note.
Forward reference to not showing off (Ench. 46–47, days 381–382) is only named, not taught.
